summary: Describes crankback signaling for MPLS and GMPLS RSVP-TE. When path setup is blocked because routing information is out of date, failure details are returned from the point of failure so a new attempt can avoid it. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: If you hit a dead end while driving, you go back and try another road. This lets a network path setup do the same, and remember the dead end.

subtitle: How a blocked MPLS or GMPLS path setup reports where it failed, so the next attempt can steer around the problem.

tldr.problem: Routing information used to compute a path can be out of date, so a label switched path setup request may hit a link or node without enough resources and be abandoned.
tldr.mechanism: The setup request carries re-routing flags that say who may retry, and the node that detects the failure returns an error with extra TLVs naming the blocked node, link or area so a repair point can compute a detour.
tldr.outcome: Setup and recovery ratios for LSPs can improve, especially when many setup requests are triggered at once. It is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no replacement.

facts.label: TLV padding
facts.value: Zero-padded to a multiple of four octets

today: RFC 4920 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the crankback TLVs and re-routing flags for RSVP-TE and GMPLS signaling.

sections.title: The Problem of Stale Routing Information
sections.content:
RFC 4920 adds crankback signaling to RSVP-TE (RFC 3209) for MPLS and to GMPLS signaling (RFC 3473). An ingress router computes an explicit path from routing data distributed by protocols such as OSPF and IS-IS. In a distributed environment that data may be out of date, so a setup request can be blocked by a link or node with insufficient resources.

Today a blocked setup produces a PathErr toward the ingress or a ResvErr toward the egress, and the setup may simply be abandoned. Crankback returns failure information from the point of failure so new attempts can avoid the blocked resources. It can also be applied to LSP recovery to show where a link or node failed.

The need is greater in GMPLS networks without wavelength converters, because the same wavelength must be allocated at each Optical Cross-Connect along an end-to-end path, which makes blocking more common.
sections.eli5: A map can be out of date, so you may drive down a road that turns out to be closed. Crankback is the closed-road sign that tells you where to turn around, so your next try goes a different way.

sections.title: Explicit Versus Implicit Re-Routing
sections.content:
Existing messages, such as the error values of PathErr and the Notify message, let a node infer that re-routing could be tried. The RFC argues this is not always desirable, since the retry may be doomed to failure. Appendix A gives an example from TDM networks, where a release message with cause value CV34 (all circuits busy) is used as an implicit re-route hint. The node receiving it cannot tell where the blocking happened, so it may retry a path that fails again, or give up when a retry would have worked.

The document therefore proposes an explicit re-routing indication and says it is best to know two things separately: where blockage or congestion occurred, and whether alternate routing should be attempted.

Crankback is also not a replacement for TE flooding. What a node learns is for recomputing the path of the same LSP, not for influencing the paths of other LSPs.
sections.eli5: Being told only that a road is busy is not much help. It is better to be told exactly where the jam is and whether trying another route is allowed.

sections.title: How Re-Routing Works
sections.content:
When setup is blocked, an error with the location of the blockage goes back to a repair point: the ingress LSR, an area border LSR, an AS border LSR or some other node. In a flat network the ingress computes an alternate path and sends a new setup request. In a network split into areas, an area border LSR may intercept and terminate the error and re-route within the downstream area. Any node may act as a repair point, though the RFC warns that this can waste network and CPU resources.

The reason for failure matters. "No Route to Destination" is likely to lead to a path that excludes the reporting LSR, while "Temporary Control Plane Congestion" may just call for a retry after a pause. When the explicit route contains loose hops or abstract nodes, the error also needs to say where in the route the problem occurred. A new route can be signaled as an Explicit Route, or as route exclusions (RFC 4874).

The repair point SHOULD keep a history table of all blockages for the LSP, so a second attempt does not repeat a path that already failed. It SHOULD discard the table with a timer no larger than the LSP retry timer on the ingress. Each repair point SHOULD apply a locally configurable limit on re-routing attempts, and when it is exceeded the failure is reported upstream.
sections.eli5: Imagine a delivery driver who writes down every blocked street. Each time they try a new way they skip all the streets on the list, and after a few tries they ask the dispatcher for help.

sections.title: Controlling Who May Retry
sections.content:
The ingress sets a Re-routing Flag on the setup request. The values are mutually exclusive and carried as bits in the LSP Attributes TLV of the LSP_ATTRIBUTES object from RFC 4420. With no flag set, the default and the backward-compatible option, only the ingress MAY re-route, and intermediate nodes SHOULD NOT.

A node that detects a failure SHOULD act according to the flag. If end-to-end re-routing is indicated, or if it chooses not to re-route, it MUST return an error and SHOULD include full crankback information. A new error code and value, Routing Problem / Re-routing limit exceeded (24/22), says that a node abandoned re-routing because it reached its retry threshold. A node receiving it MAY try crankback itself, but it is RECOMMENDED that such attempts be limited to the ingress.
sections.eli5: The sender writes on the package who is allowed to pick another route if the first one is blocked: only the sender, only the big hubs, or anyone along the way.

sections.title: The Crankback TLVs
sections.content:
Crankback information rides in the IF_ID ERROR_SPEC object of RFC 3473, on PathErr, ResvErr and Notify messages. RFC 3471 already defines TLV types 1 to 5 for interface addresses and indexes. This RFC adds types 6 to 27.

They fall into groups. The error report TLVs are types 1 to 3, and when crankback is used at least one of them MUST be present. The fundamental TLVs are types 1 to 11 (the failed interface, labels, node, area and AS) and SHOULD be supplied when the reporting node has the information. Types 8 to 11 MAY be omitted by local policy. The additional TLVs locate the fault within the path: types 12 to 20 SHOULD be supplied as appropriate, and types 21 to 27 MAY be. Types 12 and 13 give ERO context, the hop being satisfied and the next hop being reached. Types 21 to 24 describe the reporting node, and types 25 to 27 carry a proposed ERO and lists of excluded nodes and links.

Types 4 and 5 are obsoleted by RFC 4201 and SHOULD NOT be used. There is no ordering requirement among the TLVs.
sections.eli5: The error message is like a form with boxes: which street, which town, which district, and what you suggest instead. You fill in only the boxes that help.

sections.title: Receiving, Aggregating and Recovering
sections.content:
A node that receives crankback information first checks whether the Re-routing Flags let it re-route. If not, it forwards the PathErr (or, at the ingress, reports the LSP as failed). If it may re-route, it computes a path using the original explicit path while excluding the failed node or link, and signals the result as an explicit route. A node that expanded or replaced the explicit route MUST update the crankback information about the route it received, otherwise upstream nodes have little chance of routing around the problem.

When a node gives up, it MUST pass the failure upstream with crankback information. A full list of failures could get large, so TLVs 26 and 27 give a concise way to accumulate them. How aggregation is done is outside the scope of the RFC.

If a ResvErr carries crankback information to the egress, the egress MAY ignore it. If it supports crankback and local recovery has failed, it SHOULD send a PathErr with the information to the ingress. A Notify message MAY carry the information to report the error faster. For recovery of an established LSP, an LSR that sends a PathErr with the Path_State_Remove flag SHOULD also send a PathTear downstream, though with the Shared Explicit reservation style it MAY hold off to allow make-before-break repair.
sections.eli5: Whoever hears about the blocked road checks if they are allowed to choose a new route. If they are, they plan one around the list of bad roads. If not, they pass the news back to someone who can.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC introduces no change to RSVP-TE security. The RSVP-TE trust model assumes neighbors and peers exchange legitimate messages, and that trust is assumed to cascade across a network to form a trust domain. Existing authentication and message protection apply to crankback carried on PathErr and Notify.

Crankback is expected to be used between domains, so information may cross trust borders. A domain could try to thrash LSPs, or falsely report that neither it nor its downstream neighbor can provide a path, which is hard to overcome but may be detected with indirect requests to a Path Computation Element (RFC 4655). A malicious user with protocol access could use crankback information to prevent valid LSPs being established, so existing RSVP-TE security features SHOULD be made available by implementations that offer crankback, and re-routing attempt thresholds help too.
sections.eli5: The system works because neighbors trust each other to tell the truth. Someone could lie about a road being closed, so the network keeps its locks on and limits how many times it will retry.
